title: Not to be served (Mark 10:32–45)
hookLine: James and John want the best seats; he came to serve and give his life
carry: not to be served, but to serve

lines: ON THE ROAD UP TO JERUSALEM.
cards: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walks out in front. Mark says the disciples were amazed, and the ones following were afraid.

He takes the twelve aside and tells them, for the third time, and this time step by step: he'll be condemned, handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, spat on and killed, and the third day rise again.

Right then, James and John come up with a request. Their opening line is a kid asking a parent to agree before hearing the question: "Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire." What is it?
Let us sit, one on your right and one on your left, in your glory. The best seats. Reserved.

teach.h: CAN YE DRINK OF THE CUP?
teach.b: Jesus answers: you don't know what you're asking. Can you drink the cup I drink? We can, they say, quickly.
You will, he says. But the seats aren't mine to give. The other ten, Mark says, were much displeased with James and John.
So Jesus calls them all together. You know how rulers among the nations lord it over people, and the powerful throw their weight around.

teach.h: IT SHALL NOT BE SO AMONG YOU.
teach.b: But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all.
Then: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

teach.h: NOT TO BE SERVED, BUT TO SERVE.

teach.b: And today's word, ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set someone free, a captive or a slave. Christians have understood this word in different ways.
Christian tradition hears it at the heart of the cross: Jesus's death sets people free from sin.
Theologians have long asked who, if anyone, is paid; some say the picture is about the cost of freedom, not a bill handed to someone.

teach.h: TO GIVE HIS LIFE A RANSOM FOR MANY.
teach.b: The verse itself keeps the direction: the one who could claim the top seat gives his life for many. A few chapters on, Mark will show who ends up on his right and his left. It won't be what James and John had in mind.

how: Christians often call Mark 10:45 a summary of Jesus's mission, and some churches describe their ministries of service with its words; some leaders wash feet or serve meals to others as a sign of it.

o: the price paid to set a captive free
a fine paid at the temple for a sin
a gift brought to a newborn king

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: one on thy right, one on thy left
a price paid to free a captive

s: James and John asked right after he spoke of his death
the third warning, step by step, on the road.
the seats weren't his to give, he said.
all Christians agree who the ransom was paid to
theologians answer differently; some say it's about cost, not a bill.

games.q: you're James. you ask for the seat at his right hand in glory. he asks: can you drink the cup I drink? what do you say?
games.why: "We can," they say at once. he tells them they will, but the seats aren't his to give. greatness, he says, is service.

practice: Picture a place you'll be today, a table, a meeting, a car, a line, and find the best seat, the first turn, the last word.

Now picture yourself choosing the other one, on purpose, without making a show of it: the back of the line, the middle seat, serving the food before sitting down. If you pray, you can offer it as a small way of following.

wordCard.voice: Ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set a captive free. He came to give his life as a ransom for many.

orig.note: Greek: a ransom, the price paid to free a captive or a slave. from lyō, to loose.

carryVoice: Your line: not to be served, but to serve. The top seat, given away. Until tomorrow.
